plain_english: "What's the difference between me, a fool, and you, a wise person?" The difference is enormous. Rich people are servants in a wise person's house, but they're masters in a fool's house. You get used to wealth and cling to it as if someone promised it would be yours forever. But a wise person never thinks more about poverty than when surrounded by riches. No general trusts peace so much that he stops preparing for war. Even if war never comes, it's still been declared. You get arrogant about your fine house, as if it could never burn down or collapse. Wealth goes to your head, as if it's beyond all danger and too big for Fortune to destroy. You sit around playing with your money and don't see the dangers coming. You're like barbarians under siege. They don't understand siege weapons, so they watch the enemy work and don't realize what those machines are for. That's exactly what happens to you. You fall asleep over your property and never think about all the disasters waiting to attack you from every side. Soon they'll steal your expensive treasures. But if you take wealth away from a wise person, you still leave him with everything that's truly his. He lives happily in the present and fears nothing about the future.
original_excerpt: "What difference, then, is there between me, who am a fool, and you, who are a wise man?" "All the difference in the world: for riches are slaves in the house of a wise man, but masters in that of a fool. You accustom yourself to them and cling to them as if somebody had promised that they should be yours for ever, but a wise man never thinks so much about poverty as when he is surrounded by riches. No general ever trusts so implicitly in the maintenance of peace as not to make himself ready for a war, which, though it may not actually be waged, has nevertheless been declared; you are rendered over-proud by a fine house, as though it could never be burned or fall down, and your heads are turned by riches as though they were beyond the reach of all dangers and were so great that Fortune has not sufficient strength to swallow them up. You sit idly playing with your wealth and do not foresee the perils in store for it, as savages generally do when besieged, for, not understanding the use of siege artillery, they look on idly at the labours of the besiegers and do not understand the object of the machines which they are putting together at a distance: and this is exactly what happens to you: you go to sleep over your property, and never reflect how many misfortunes loom menacingly around you on all sides, and soon will plunder you of costly spoils, but if one takes away riches from the wise man, one leaves him still in possession of all that is his: for he lives happy in the present, and without fear for the future."

plain_english: The great Socrates, or anyone else with the same strength to rise above worldly things, would say: 'I have one firm rule — I will not change how I live to fit your biases. You can pour all your usual complaints on me from every direction. I won't think you're attacking me. You're just crying like little babies.' This is what a wise person would say. His mind is free from vice, so he corrects others — not because he hates them, but to help them improve. And he would add: 'Your opinion of me causes me pain, but not for my sake — for yours. To hate what is good and attack virtue means giving up all hope of doing well yourself. You cannot harm me. People don't harm the gods when they tear down altars either. But your intention is clearly evil, and you want to do damage even when you can't. I put up with your chatter the same way Jupiter puts up with poets' silly stories. One poet gives him wings, another horns. One makes him an adulterer who stays out all night. Another shows him being cruel to the gods or unfair to people. Another makes him seduce noble young men and kidnap them by force — even his own relatives. Another calls him a father-killer who stole someone else's kingdom from his own father.'
original_excerpt: "The great Socrates, or any one else who had the same superiority to and power to withstand the things of this life, would say, 'I have no more fixed principle than that of not altering the course of my life to suit your prejudices: you may pour your accustomed talk upon me from all sides: I shall not think that you are abusing me, but that you are merely wailing like poor little babies.'" This is what the man will say who possesses wisdom, whose mind, being free from vices, bids him reproach others, not because he hates them, but in order to improve them: and to this he will add, "Your opinion of me affects me with pain, not for my own sake but for yours, because to hate perfection and to assail virtue is in itself a resignation of all hope of doing well. You do me no harm; neither do men harm the gods when they overthrow their altars: but it is clear that your intention is an evil one and that you will wish to do harm even where you are not able."

plain_english: The only result of such stories is that people feel less ashamed of doing wrong. They think it's okay because the gods supposedly did it too. Even though your behavior doesn't harm me personally, I still want to give you some advice for your own good: respect virtue. Listen to those who have followed virtue for years. They'll tell you it's incredibly powerful — and it gets stronger every day. Treat virtue like you would treat the gods. Respect virtue's followers like you would respect priests. And whenever anyone talks about sacred teachings, _favete linguis_ — give us your respectful silence. Most people think this phrase comes from the word "favor," but it actually means "be quiet." It's a command for silence so divine service can happen without being interrupted by unlucky words. You need this reminder even more. When the oracle speaks, you should listen carefully and quietly. But look what you actually do. When someone shakes a rattle and claims a god told them to do it, you gather around. When some fake holy man cuts his arms and shoulders to make them bleed, you watch. When someone crawls down the street on their knees howling, or when some old man in linen robes comes out during the day carrying a lamp and laurel branch, shouting that a god is angry — you crowd around him and hang on every word. You all feed each other's amazement, declaring that he must be divinely inspired.
original_excerpt: "I bear with your prating in the same spirit in which Jupiter, best and greatest, bears with the idle tales of the poets, one of whom represents him with wings, another with horns, another as an adulterer staying out all night, another is dealing harshly with the gods, another as unjust to men, another as the seducer of noble youths whom he carries off by force, and those, too, his own relatives, another as a parricide and the conqueror of another's kingdom, and that his father's. The only result of such tales is that men feel less shame at committing sin if they believe the gods to be guilty of such actions. But although this conduct of yours does not hurt me, yet, for your own sakes, I advise you, respect virtue: believe those who having long followed her cry aloud that what they follow is a thing of might, and daily appears mightier. Reverence her as you would the gods, and reverence her followers as you would the priests of the gods: and whenever any mention of sacred writings is made, _favete linguis_, favour us with silence: this word is not derived, as most people imagine, from _favour_, but commands silence, that divine service may be performed without being interrupted by any words of evil omen."

plain_english: You need to be told to do this so that when the real oracle speaks, you'll pay attention and listen quietly. But look what happens instead: whenever someone shakes a rattle and claims a god told them to do it, or when some faker cuts his arms and shoulders to make himself bleed, or when someone crawls down the street on his knees howling, or when some old man in white robes comes out in broad daylight carrying a lamp and a laurel branch, shouting that a god is angry — you all crowd around him. You hang on his every word. You make each other even more amazed by insisting he must be inspired by the gods.
original_excerpt: "It is much more necessary that you should be ordered to do this, in order that whenever utterance is made by that oracle, you may listen to it with attention and in silence. Whenever any one beats a sistrum,[6] pretending to do so by divine command, any proficient in grazing his own skin covers his arms and shoulders with blood from light cuts, any one crawls on his knees howling along the street, or any old man clad in linen comes forth in daylight with a lamp and laurel branch and cries out that one of the gods is angry, you crowd round him and listen to his words, and each increases the other's wonderment by declaring him to be divinely inspired."
